steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a stencil computation algorithm built on vector outer product instructions of matrix accelerator units, covering the hardware background, related stencil work, our approach, contributions and paper outline.

  - no stencil algorithm for vector outer product accelerator
- Gather vs. scatter
  - gather view: output = sum of neighbor inputs; hard to use outer products
  - scatter view: update pattern of one input element; used for data reuse and register spilling
- This paper
  - novel stencil algorithm with vector outer products, from scatter mode
  - 2D first, then other stencil types via key concept; theoretical analysis
  - optimizations: memory reference pattern, execution pipeline, data reuse
  - contributions: algorithm + theory; implementation + automatic code generator; evaluation on 2D and 3D stencils
  - outline: Sections 2–7

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Processors have recently been equipped with matrix registers and associated operations, as powerful units for accelerating modern AI and high-performance computing applications. Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) is a fundamental computation pattern in these applications, so many commercial hardware accelerators, like NVIDIA Tensor Cores, Google TPUs and Intel AMXs, have been designed with matrix-matrix multiplication instructions which offer O(n^{3}) arithmetic operations with O(n^{2}) operands. The arithmetic density, i.e, the number of floating point operations performed per byte, is O(n), which is one order of magnitude greater than other traditional instructions.

GEMM can be implemented with inner products or with outer products, as is well-known. Some architectures have inner product instructions, e.g., ARMv8.4. But it only completes O(n) arithmetic operations. The outer product instead performs O(n^{2}) calculations in a single instruction. It can also be used as the building block for other computations such as triangular solvers. Several architectures have proposed outer product accelerator units in their processors, like the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME) in ARM and the Math Matrix Accelerator (MMA) in IBM Power10.

The outer product takes two vectors and produces a matrix, and each element of the output matrix is a product of the corresponding values in the two input vectors. The outer product is clearly more lightweight than matrix multiplication. It gives more opportunities to develop flexible algorithms for more problems other than dense linear algebra computing, and more possibilities to optimize the instruction pipelines, data organization and data reuse among input vectors.

Stencil computation is one of the thirteen Berkeley motifs. It represents a very common class of nested loops in scientific and engineering applications, dynamic programming, and image processing algorithms. Stencils can be classified by the dimension of the space grid (1D, 2D…), the shape (box, star…) and the order.

Existing work on stencil computation mainly focuses on tiling, parallelization and vectorization. Some works discuss stencil algorithms on GPU and other many-core processors, and the transformation of stencil computation to matrix multiplications. As far as we know, there is no stencil algorithm that targets the vector outer product accelerator.

- Gather vs. scatter view
  - gather: each output = sum of neighbor inputs; hard to use outer products
  - scatter: update pattern of one input element; used for data reuse, register spilling (single dimension / single element)
- This paper
  - novel stencil algorithm using vector outer products, from scatter mode
  - 2D stencil first, then other types via key concept; theoretical analysis
  - optimizations for memory reference pattern, execution pipeline, data reuse
- Contributions: algorithm + theory; implementation, optimizations, automatic code generator; performance over 2D and 3D stencils
- Organization: Sec 2 background, Sec 3 algorithm + analysis, Sec 4 optimizations, Sec 5 evaluation on simulator, Sec 6 related work, Sec 7 summary

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Processors have recently been equipped with matrix registers and associated operations, as powerful units for accelerating modern AI and high-performance computing applications. Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) is a fundamental computation pattern in these applications, so many commercial hardware accelerators, like NVIDIA Tensor Cores, Google TPUs and Intel AMXs, have been designed with matrix-matrix multiplication instructions which offer O(n^{3}) arithmetic operations with O(n^{2}) operands. The arithmetic density, i.e, the number of floating point operations performed per byte, is O(n), which is one order of magnitude greater than other traditional instructions.

GEMM can be implemented with inner products or with outer products, as is well-known. Some architectures have inner product instructions, e.g., ARMv8.4. But it only completes O(n) arithmetic operations. The outer product instead performs O(n^{2}) calculations in a single instruction. It can also be used as the building block for other computations such as triangular solvers. Several architectures have proposed outer product accelerator units in their processors, like the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME) in ARM and the Math Matrix Accelerator (MMA) in IBM Power10.

The outer product takes two vectors and produces a matrix, and each element of the output matrix is a product of the corresponding values in the two input vectors. The outer product is clearly more lightweight than matrix multiplication. It gives more opportunities to develop flexible algorithms for more problems other than dense linear algebra computing, and more possibilities to optimize the instruction pipelines, data organization and data reuse among input vectors.

Stencil computation is one of the thirteen Berkeley motifs. It represents a very common class of nested loops in scientific and engineering applications, dynamic programming, and image processing algorithms. Stencils can be classified by the dimension of the space grid (1D, 2D…), the shape (box, star…) and the order.

Existing work on stencil computation mainly focuses on tiling, parallelization and vectorization. Some works discuss stencil algorithms on GPU and other many-core processors, and the transformation of stencil computation to matrix multiplications. As far as we know, there is no stencil algorithm that targets the vector outer product accelerator.

Most of the existing work uses the conventional gather view of a stencil definition, where each output element is calculated by summing its neighbor input elements. With this perspective it is difficult to use outer products for stencil computations. The scatter view of a stencil describes how one single input element updates. This view has been used for fine-grained in-core optimizations, e.g., improving data reuse and eliminating register spilling, by combining the gather and scatter views for a single dimension and a single element, respectively.

In this paper we propose a new stencil algorithm using vector outer products. Unlike previous work, the algorithm comes from the stencil definition in the scatter mode. The algorithm for a 2D stencil is first expressed with formulas of vector outer products through a series of extensions to the scatter mode. Then it is adapted to other stencil types by identifying a key concept underlying the algorithm, and we also analyze it theoretically with respect to this concept. The implementation has a set of optimizations to improve the memory reference pattern, execution pipeline and data reuse, considering various algorithmic options and the data sharing between input vectors. The contributions of this paper are:

- We propose a stencil algorithm using vector outer products, and we analyze the theoretical aspects of the algorithm.

- We implement the algorithm with a set of optimizations to boost the in-core performance, and we design an automatic code generator.

- We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is effective, with substantial performance improvement over a range of 2D and 3D stencils.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 gives some background on matrix accelerator units and stencil computations. Section 3 describes the stencil algorithm that uses vector outer product operations and gives a detailed theoretical analysis. Section 4 presents optimizations on memory reference and data reuse. Section 5 evaluates performance on a simulator with various 2D and 3D stencils. Section 6 reviews related work and Section 7 summarizes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Matrix registers and associated operations have recently been equipped in processors as powerful units for accelerating modern AI and high-performance computing applications. As Matrix Multiplication (GEMM) is a fundamental computation pattern in these applications, many commercial hardware accelerators, such as NVIDIA Tensor Cores [1], Google TPUs [2] and Intel AMXs [3], have been designed to incorporate matrix-matrix multiplication instructions offering O(n^{3}) arithmetic operations with O(n^{2}) operands. The arithmetic density, i.e, the number of floating point operations performed per byte, is O(n), one order of magnitude greater than that of other traditional instructions.

It is well-known that GEMM can be implemented with inner products or outer products. Inner product instructions exist in some architectures, e.g., ARMv8.4, but they only complete O(n) arithmetic operations. On the contrary, the outer product performs O(n^{2}) calculations in a single instruction, and it can also be used as the building block of other computations such as triangular solvers. Several architectures have proposed outer product accelerator units in their processors, such as the Scalable Matrix Extension (SME) in ARM [4] and the Math Matrix Accelerator (MMA) in IBM Power10 [5].

The outer product is fed with two vectors and produces a matrix, in which each element is a product of corresponding values in the two input vectors. The outer product is clearly more lightweight than matrix multiplication. It provides more opportunities to develop flexible algorithms for problems other than dense linear algebra computing, and more possibilities to optimize the instruction pipelines, data organization and data reuse among input vectors.

The stencil computation is identified as one of the thirteen Berkeley motifs [6] and represents a very common class of nested loops in scientific and engineering applications, dynamic programming, and image processing algorithms. Stencils can be classified in terms of the dimension of the space grid (1D, 2D…), the shape (box, star…) and the order.

Existing work on stencil computation mainly focuses on tiling [7,8,9], parallelization [10,11,12] and vectorization [13,14,15]. Several works discuss stencil algorithms on GPU [16,17,18] and other many-core processors [19], as well as the transformation of stencil computation to matrix multiplications [20,21]. To the best of our knowledge, no stencil algorithm targets the vector outer product accelerator.

Most of the existing work adopts the conventional gather view of a stencil definition, where each output element is calculated by summing its neighbor input elements. This perspective makes it difficult to utilize outer products for stencil computations. The scatter view of a stencil [22] instead describes the updating pattern of one single input element. This standpoint has been used for fine-grained in-core optimizations, e.g., improving data reuse [23] and eliminating register spilling [24] by combining the gather and scatter views for a single dimension and a single element, respectively.

This paper proposes a novel stencil algorithm using vector outer products. Unlike previous work, the new algorithm arises from the stencil definition in the scatter mode. The algorithm for a 2D stencil is first expressed with formulas of vector outer products through a series of extensions to the scatter mode. It is then adapted to other stencil types by identifying a key concept underlying the algorithm, and it is also analyzed theoretically with respect to this concept. The implementation incorporates a set of optimizations to improve the memory reference pattern, execution pipeline and data reuse by considering various algorithmic options and the data sharing between input vectors. This paper makes the following contributions:

- • We propose a stencil algorithm using vector outer products and analyze its theoretical aspects.

- • We implement the algorithm with a set of optimizations to boost the in-core performance, and we design an automatic code generator.

- • We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, showing substantial performance improvement over a range of 2D and 3D stencils.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background on matrix accelerator units and stencil computations. Section 3 describes the stencil algorithm that utilizes vector outer product operations and offers a detailed theoretical analysis. Section 4 presents a set of optimizations on the memory reference and data reuse. Section 5 evaluates the performance on a simulator using various 2D and 3D stencils. Section 6 reviews related work and Section 7 summarizes the paper.
